Pilar 7 — Bayesian Hierarchical Spatial Models

Hugo Rodrigues

Source: vignettes/pilar7-bayesian-hierarchical.Rmd
pilar7-bayesian-hierarchical.Rmd

Abstract

A machine-learning soil map returns a number at every pixel. It rarely returns an honest interval around that number, because the residual spatial structure the model failed to explain is treated as noise rather than as a signal with a covariance. Pillar 7 takes the opposite route: it puts the spatial dependence inside the model, as a Gaussian process random effect, and returns a full posterior over every quantity of interest (Banerjee et al. 2014; Cressie and Wikle 2011).

This vignette derives the hierarchy, is explicit about the one non-conjugate parameter and the concession edaphos makes for it, and then spends most of its length on the part that is usually skipped: the two diagnostics that decide whether the fitted spatial field means anything at all.

1. The hierarchy

Write the observed soil property at site sis_i as a mean structure plus a spatially correlated random effect plus independent error:

y(si)=𝐱(si)⊤𝛃+w(si)+ε(si),i=1,…,n. y(s_i) \;=\; \mathbf{x}(s_i)^\top \boldsymbol\beta \;+\; w(s_i) \;+\; \varepsilon(s_i), \qquad i = 1,\dots,n .

The three layers are

data:y∣𝛃,w,τ2∼N(X𝛃+w,τ2I)process:w∣σ2,ϕ∼N(0,σ2R(ϕ))priors:𝛃∼N(0,vβI),σ2∼IG(a,b),τ2∼IG(a,b) \begin{aligned} \text{data:} \quad & y \mid \boldsymbol\beta, w, \tau^2 \;\sim\; N(X\boldsymbol\beta + w,\; \tau^2 I) \\ \text{process:} \quad & w \mid \sigma^2, \phi \;\sim\; N(0,\; \sigma^2 R(\phi)) \\ \text{priors:} \quad & \boldsymbol\beta \sim N(0, v_\beta I), \quad \sigma^2 \sim IG(a, b), \quad \tau^2 \sim IG(a, b) \end{aligned}

with an exponential correlation function

R(ϕ)ij=exp⁡(−ϕ‖si−sj‖). R(\phi)_{ij} \;=\; \exp\!\big(-\phi \, \lVert s_i - s_j \rVert\big).

Note the parameterisation carefully, because it is the source of most mistakes with this model: ϕ\phi is a decay rate, not a range. Its units are 1/distance. Large ϕ\phi means correlation dies off quickly; ϕ→∞\phi \to \infty drives R→IR \to I. The practical correlation range is roughly 3/ϕ3/\phi. If your coordinates are in degrees, a sensible ϕ\phi is a very different number than if they are in metres.

τ2\tau^2 is the nugget: variation below the shortest sampling distance, pooling laboratory error and micro-scale heterogeneity. σ2\sigma^2 is the partial sill, the variance of the structured field.

1.1 Why ϕ\phi is the hard one

Collapse ww out of the likelihood:

y∣𝛃,σ2,τ2,ϕ∼N(X𝛃,Σ),Σ=σ2R(ϕ)+τ2I. y \mid \boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2, \tau^2, \phi \;\sim\; N\!\left(X\boldsymbol\beta,\; \Sigma\right), \qquad \Sigma = \sigma^2 R(\phi) + \tau^2 I .

Conditional on ϕ\phi this is an ordinary Bayesian linear model with a known covariance: 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta has a Gaussian full conditional and the variances have inverse-gamma full conditionals. Every update is closed-form.

But ϕ\phi sits inside a matrix inverse and a determinant. It has no conjugate update, and a Metropolis step on it pays an O(n3)O(n^3) Cholesky for every proposal, accepted or rejected.

edaphos avoids the Metropolis step. It profiles ϕ\phi: over the bracket phi_range it maximises the marginal likelihood once, fixes ϕ\phi at ϕ̂\hat\phi, and runs a fully conjugate Gibbs sampler for everything else. This is the concession INLA makes for its hyperparameters (Rue et al. 2009) — treat the rate as estimated rather than sampled, buy exact fast updates for the parameters you report.

The cost, stated plainly: the reported posterior for 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta is conditional on ϕ̂\hat\phi and does not propagate uncertainty in the rate. It is a conditional posterior, not a joint one.

2. The Cerrado grid

br_cerrado is a 45 × 45 regular grid of synthesised Cerrado observations bundled with the package, so this vignette runs offline and identically everywhere.

data(br_cerrado)
str(br_cerrado)
#> 'data.frame':    2025 obs. of  8 variables:
#>  $ x     : num  -48 -47.9 -47.9 -47.9 -47.9 ...
#>  $ y     : num  -16 -16 -16 -16 -16 -16 -16 -16 -16 -16 ...
#>  $ elev  : num  904 928 900 912 934 ...
#>  $ slope : num  2.59 9.9 14.19 6.23 11.89 ...
#>  $ twi   : num  10.32 11.23 11.47 11.28 8.12 ...
#>  $ map_mm: num  1197 1239 1209 1160 1225 ...
#>  $ ndvi  : num  0.719 0.619 0.531 0.586 0.517 0.648 0.668 0.529 0.648 0.693 ...
#>  $ soc   : num  27.6 20.1 20.2 17.2 15.7 ...
set.seed(42)
idx   <- sample(nrow(br_cerrado), 220)
train <- br_cerrado[idx, ]
test  <- br_cerrado[-idx, ][sample(nrow(br_cerrado) - 220, 200), ]

c(n_train = nrow(train), n_test = nrow(test))
#> n_train  n_test 
#>     220     200

The Gibbs sampler is O(n3)O(n^3) per iteration through the Cholesky, so nn — not the iteration count — is what binds on a laptop.

3. Fit the full model, and read the warning 

fit_full <- bhs_fit(
  data      = train,
  formula   = soc ~ elev + slope + twi + map_mm,
  coords    = c("x", "y"),
  backend   = "gibbs",
  nmcmc     = 1500L, burn = 500L, thin = 2L,
  phi_range = c(0.05, 1000),
  seed      = 1L, verbose = FALSE
)
#> Warning: bhs_fit(): the profile-MLE of phi (1000) is at the upper end of
#> phi_range = c(0.05, 1000), supplied. Widen phi_range and refit; the spatial
#> variance fraction is not trustworthy until phi is interior. phi is a rate
#> (1/distance) in the units of `coords`.

That warning is not noise to be silenced. It is the first diagnostic.

bhs_fit() warns when ϕ̂\hat\phi lands on an endpoint of phi_range, because then the bracket — not the data — determined the answer. Here the likelihood is still climbing at the upper end: it wants ϕ\phi as large as it can get, which is the model’s way of saying there is no residual spatial structure left to fit. Every driver of soc in this synthesised grid is already in the formula, so the residual is white.

Widening the bracket will not help; it will rail again, further out. The right conclusion is that a spatial random effect is not needed for this specification.

3.1 The diagnostic that works, and the one that does not

The number most often quoted from a fit like this is the spatial fraction σ2/(σ2+τ2)\sigma^2 / (\sigma^2 + \tau^2). This section shows why, on its own, it tells you nothing.

The question a spatial model has to answer first is whether the fitted correlation is resolvable by the sampling design at all. The practical range is 3/ϕ3/\phi; compare it to the shortest distance between two sampled sites:

d_min <- min(dist(train[, c("x", "y")]))

c(phi_hat       = fit_full$phi_hat,
  range_3_over  = 3 / fit_full$phi_hat,
  d_min         = d_min,
  range_per_dmin = (3 / fit_full$phi_hat) / d_min,
  corr_nearest  = exp(-fit_full$phi_hat * d_min))
#>        phi_hat   range_3_over          d_min range_per_dmin   corr_nearest 
#>   9.999999e+02   3.000000e-03   6.818182e-03   4.400000e-01   1.093708e-03

The fitted range is shorter than the gap between the two closest observations. Nothing in the design can see structure at that scale: even nearest neighbours are essentially uncorrelated, so RR is numerically the identity and Σ=σ2R+τ2I≈(σ2+τ2)I\Sigma = \sigma^2 R + \tau^2 I \approx (\sigma^2 + \tau^2) I. In that regime ww and ε\varepsilon enter the likelihood identically — they are aliased, and only their sum is a statement about the data.

Now look at the spatial fraction anyway:

fr_full <- fit_full$sigma2_draws /
           (fit_full$sigma2_draws + fit_full$tau2_draws)
c(mean = mean(fr_full), sd = sd(fr_full))
#>       mean         sd 
#> 0.96647675 0.02487572

Near 1, with a tight posterior — which reads as “almost all residual variance is spatially structured” and is the opposite of the truth. The apparent precision is the trap: a narrow posterior on an aliased quantity is not evidence. Section 4 fits a model where the field is real and shows this same number barely moves, which is the point.

4. Omit a driver, and the field reappears

A GP random effect is, operationally, a surrogate for spatially smooth predictors you do not have. We can demonstrate that directly by dropping map_mm — a smooth climate driver — and refitting.

fit_drop <- bhs_fit(
  data      = train,
  formula   = soc ~ elev + slope + twi,
  coords    = c("x", "y"),
  backend   = "gibbs",
  nmcmc     = 1500L, burn = 500L, thin = 2L,
  phi_range = c(0.05, 1000),
  seed      = 1L, verbose = FALSE
)

c(phi_hat        = fit_drop$phi_hat,
  interior       = fit_drop$phi_hat < 1000,
  range_3_over   = 3 / fit_drop$phi_hat,
  range_per_dmin = (3 / fit_drop$phi_hat) / d_min,
  corr_nearest   = exp(-fit_drop$phi_hat * d_min))
#>        phi_hat       interior   range_3_over range_per_dmin   corr_nearest 
#>   130.33663481     1.00000000     0.02301732     3.37587356     0.41120686

No warning this time: ϕ̂\hat\phi is interior, so the data — not the bracket — chose it. And the range now spans several nearest-neighbour spacings, with immediate neighbours meaningfully correlated. This is a real, short-range field: the GP has taken over the job the omitted rainfall covariate was doing.

That is the honest interpretation of a spatial random effect in any applied fit — it is as much a statement about what is missing from your covariate stack as about pedogenesis.

Now the promised comparison. Here is the spatial fraction for this fit, where the field is genuine:

fr_drop <- fit_drop$sigma2_draws /
           (fit_drop$sigma2_draws + fit_drop$tau2_draws)

rbind(`full (no resolvable field)` = c(mean = mean(fr_full), sd = sd(fr_full)),
      `reduced (real field)`       = c(mean = mean(fr_drop), sd = sd(fr_drop)))
#>                                 mean         sd
#> full (no resolvable field) 0.9664767 0.02487572
#> reduced (real field)       0.9661160 0.02463437

The two are practically indistinguishable — same value, same tight posterior — yet one fit has a resolvable spatial field and the other has none. The spatial fraction did not detect the difference. What did was ϕ̂\hat\phi: interior versus railed, and its range measured against the sampling distance.

Report those together, or report neither.

round(t(apply(fit_drop$beta_draws, 2, function(b)
  c(mean = mean(b), sd = sd(b),
    q025 = quantile(b, 0.025, names = FALSE),
    q975 = quantile(b, 0.975, names = FALSE)))), 4)
#>                mean     sd     q025    q975
#> (Intercept) -9.6390 9.5736 -29.0979  7.3221
#> elev         0.0210 0.0078   0.0080  0.0375
#> slope       -0.5838 0.0508  -0.6791 -0.4846
#> twi          1.8848 0.2537   1.4221  2.3367

A coefficient whose 95% credible interval excludes zero is one the data resolve after the field has absorbed everything it can — a stricter bar than an OLS pp-value, because a covariate that merely happens to be smooth in space will have its apparent effect soaked up by ww.

5. Bayesian kriging, and whether the interval is earned

Prediction at a new site is not 𝐱0⊤𝛃̂\mathbf{x}_0^\top \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}. Marginalising the field out of the hierarchy gives the exact Gaussian conditional

E[y0∣y]=𝐱0⊤𝛃+σ2𝐫0⊤Σ−1(y−X𝛃),V[y0∣y]=σ2+τ2⏟marginal−σ4𝐫0⊤Σ−1𝐫0⏟kriging variance, \begin{aligned} E[y_0 \mid y] &= \mathbf{x}_0^\top \boldsymbol\beta + \sigma^2 \mathbf{r}_0^\top \Sigma^{-1} (y - X\boldsymbol\beta), \\ V[y_0 \mid y] &= \underbrace{\sigma^2 + \tau^2}_{\text{marginal}} - \underbrace{\sigma^4 \mathbf{r}_0^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{r}_0}_{\text{kriging variance}}, \end{aligned}

evaluated at every retained posterior draw of (𝛃,σ2,τ2)(\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2, \tau^2).

The second variance term is what makes the interval location-aware. It is largest — so the subtraction is largest, so the interval is narrowest — at sites surrounded by data, and it vanishes as 𝐫0→0\mathbf{r}_0 \to 0, correctly relaxing the predictive variance to the full marginal σ2+τ2\sigma^2 + \tau^2 far from any observation. You can watch both limits:

p_at  <- predict(fit_drop, newdata = train, n_draws = 1000L)  # on the data
far   <- test[1:50, ];  far$x <- far$x + 500                  # far outside
p_far <- predict(fit_drop, newdata = far, n_draws = 1000L)

s2 <- mean(fit_drop$sigma2_draws); t2 <- mean(fit_drop$tau2_draws)
c(sd_at_observed = mean(p_at$sd),
  sd_far_away    = mean(p_far$sd),
  sqrt_marginal  = sqrt(s2 + t2))
#> sd_at_observed    sd_far_away  sqrt_marginal 
#>       1.242871       4.879549       4.850063

sd_far_away should land on sqrt_marginal, and sd_at_observed should sit well below it. An implementation that adds only the nugget would return the same small number in both columns — narrow intervals everywhere, including where the model knows nothing.

5.1 Coverage 

pred    <- predict(fit_drop, newdata = test)
covered <- test$soc >= pred$q025 & test$soc <= pred$q975

c(picp_95    = mean(covered),
  mean_width = mean(pred$q975 - pred$q025),
  rmse       = sqrt(mean((test$soc - pred$mean)^2)),
  r2         = 1 - sum((test$soc - pred$mean)^2) /
                   sum((test$soc - mean(train$soc))^2))
#>    picp_95 mean_width       rmse         r2 
#>  0.9200000 18.0049470  4.5371664  0.5702749

Read coverage and width together, never separately. An interval from −∞-\infty to ∞\infty has perfect coverage; a degenerate one has perfect width. A model earns trust when coverage lands near nominal while the width stays narrow enough to inform a decision.

Note the R2R^2 denominator: the training mean, not the test-set mean. Scoring against the test mean measures the model against an oracle no deployed map has, and inflates R2R^2 for free.

6. Where this connects

bhs_fit() returns an object the package’s unified uncertainty layer understands, so the same calibration diagnostic applies here as to every other pillar:

post <- as_edaphos_posterior(fit_drop)
class(post)
#> [1] "edaphos_posterior"

See vignette("uncertainty-unified") for the cross-pillar comparison and vignette("capstone-cerrado-campaign") for this model inside a full sampling-campaign decision.

7. Limitations

  • ϕ\phi is profiled, not sampled (§1.1); posteriors are conditional on ϕ̂\hat\phi. Always check the warning before reading the variance split (§3.1).
  • The exponential correlation is isotropic. Anisotropic pedogenesis — a catena down a slope — is not represented.
  • The O(n3)O(n^3) Cholesky bounds practical nn to the low thousands. The RcppArmadillo backend moves the constant, not the exponent.
  • br_cerrado is synthesised. The numbers above demonstrate machinery, not a published finding about the Cerrado. For real WoSIS profiles see vignette("case-cerrado-end-to-end").

References

Banerjee, Sudipto, Bradley P. Carlin, and Alan E. Gelfand. 2014. Hierarchical Modeling and Analysis for Spatial Data. 2nd ed. Chapman; Hall/CRC. https://doi.org/10.1201/b17115.
Cressie, N., and C. K. Wikle. 2011. Statistics for Spatio-Temporal Data. Wiley.
Rue, Håvard, Sara Martino, and Nicolas Chopin. 2009. “Approximate Bayesian Inference for Latent Gaussian Models by Using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximations.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 71 (2): 319–92. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00700.x.
